text: Train the same model twice and you can get two quite different scores. A 2020 paper by Dodge and colleagues measured how big that gap gets, and what it means for research results.
Here’s a small neural network. The grey layers stand in for a pretrained model like BERT, which already learned general English from billions of words.
We fine-tune it for one narrow task, like deciding whether two sentences mean the same thing. It trains on 64 examples and gets tested on 400 it hasn’t seen.
The task needs a new output layer, and its weights start out random. Blue for positive, red for negative.
The training examples also get shuffled into a random order.
Both of those random choices come from one number, the seed.
Here’s training with seed 1. The model goes through the examples six times, in a fresh order each pass, and every weight shifts a little, the pretrained ones included.
It gets 78% of the test examples right. That’s the orange dot.
Now we keep everything else the same and only change the seed.
Here are a hundred seeds.
Each dot is one full training run, and the seed is the only difference between them.
The worst run scored 60.8%, the best 82.5%. That’s a 21.7-point spread from the seed alone.
The paper found the same with BERT, over 2,100 runs on four tasks. On the smaller datasets, some runs failed completely.
The seed controls two things, so which one is responsible? The paper gave each its own seed and varied them one at a time.
Same starting weights every run, and only the order changes.
Accuracy still moves 11.2 points.
Now the same order every run, and only the starting weights change.
19.0 points. Both matter, and in the paper they mattered about equally on average.
That’s a problem for research, because papers usually report one number, not a hundred.
Say method A reports a single run, and method B reports its best of twenty.
B comes out 6.2 points ahead and looks like the better method.
This happens with published results. On a benchmark called MRPC,
BERT’s best run out of 625 seeds beat the reported scores of XLNet, RoBERTa and ALBERT, newer models that were reported as better. Those models weren’t given 625 tries.
Back to A and B. Give A twenty tries as well,
and the gap disappears. They were the same method, and B just had more tries.
So the paper says to compare methods at the same number of tries.
More tries cost more compute, so the paper also suggests a cheaper way to search: start lots of runs and stop most of them early.
Here are all 100 runs as they train. A quarter of the way in, we keep the top 30 and stop the rest.
The run that ends up best is among the 30 we kept, and the search cost about 48 runs’ worth of training instead of 100.
With BERT, the paper found weak runs often show it within the first epoch, and stopping them early gave small but consistent gains for the same compute.
So when you see a single score, it’s worth asking how many seeds it took to get it.
